metadata.title: [10A] The Sine Rule, Cosine Rule, and Triangle Area Formula
metadata.vcaa_description: Establish and apply the sine, cosine and area rules for any triangle and solve related problems in 2 and 3 dimensions.
metadata.target_mastery: Apply the Sine Rule (including the obtuse-angle ambiguous case), the Cosine Rule, and the trigonometric area formula $A = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ to solve non-right-angled triangles.

key_vocabulary.definition: In any triangle $\triangle ABC$ with sides $a, b, c$ opposite angles $A, B, C$, the ratio of each side length to the sine of its opposite angle is constant: $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}$.

key_vocabulary.term: Ambiguous case of the Sine Rule (SSA)
key_vocabulary.definition: When given two sides and a non-included acute angle (SSA), because $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$, an unknown angle $\theta$ found via $\sin\theta = k$ may have two valid solutions: an acute angle $\theta_1$ and its supplementary obtuse angle $\theta_2 = 180^\circ - \theta_1$.
A generalisation of Pythagoras' theorem to any triangle $\triangle ABC$: $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$, which rearranges to $\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}$ when all three sides are known.

The angle sandwiched directly between two known sides of a triangle (e.g., angle $C$ is the included angle between sides $a$ and $b$), used in both the Cosine Rule (SAS) and the area formula $A = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$.

theory.title: The Sine Rule and the Ambiguous Case
theory.explanation: By dropping a perpendicular altitude $h$ from vertex $C$ onto side $c$ in any triangle $\triangle ABC$, we observe $h = b\sin A$ and $h = a\sin B$, so $b\sin A = a\sin B$, which divides to give the Sine Rule. Use the Sine Rule whenever you know a matching opposite pair $(a, A)$ plus one other side or angle. When solving for an unknown angle using two sides and a non-included acute angle (SSA), always check whether the supplementary obtuse angle $\theta_2 = 180^\circ - \theta_1$ also fits inside the $180^\circ$ angle sum of the triangle.
theory.formula_latex: \frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C} \qquad \text{or} \qquad \frac{\sin A}{a} = \frac{\sin B}{b} = \frac{\sin C}{c}
theory.callout_title: Put the Unknown in the Numerator
theory.callout_rule: Put side lengths on top ($\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B}$) when finding an unknown side; flip the fractions ($\frac{\sin A}{a} = \frac{\sin B}{b}$) when finding an unknown angle.

theory.title: The Cosine Rule for SAS and SSS Triangles
theory.explanation: When no matching opposite side-angle pair is known, the Sine Rule cannot start. Instead, apply the Cosine Rule in two situations: (1) SAS — two sides and the included angle between them are known ($c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$), or (2) SSS — all three sides are known ($\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}$). Notice that when $C = 90^\circ$, $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ and the Cosine Rule reduces directly to Pythagoras' theorem $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$; furthermore, if $a^2 + b^2 - c^2 < 0$, then $\cos C < 0$ and the Cosine Rule automatically identifies $C$ as an obtuse angle ($90^\circ < C < 180^\circ$).
theory.formula_latex: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C \iff \cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}
theory.callout_title: Negative Cosine Means an Obtuse Angle
theory.callout_rule: Unlike the Sine Rule, the Cosine Rule is never ambiguous for angles between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$: if $\cos C < 0$, your calculator immediately returns the obtuse angle $C > 90^\circ$.

theory.title: The Trigonometric Area Formula for Any Triangle
theory.explanation: In any triangle $\triangle ABC$ with base $a$ and adjacent side $b$ separated by an included angle $C$, the perpendicular height is $h = b\sin C$. Substituting $h = b\sin C$ into $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$ yields $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$. This formula works for both acute and obtuse included angles without needing to construct an altitude.
theory.callout_title: Two Sides and the Angle Sandwiched Between Them
theory.callout_rule: To use $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, the two sides $a$ and $b$ MUST meet at the vertex of the known angle $C$.

worked_examples.title: Using the Sine Rule and Resolving the Ambiguous Case
worked_examples.problem: (a) In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 45^\circ$, $B = 60^\circ$, and $a = 10\text{ cm}$. Find the exact length of side $b$. (b) In $\triangle PQR$, $P = 30^\circ$, $p = 6\text{ cm}$, and $q = 6\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}$. Find the two possible values of $\angle Q$ (the acute and obtuse solutions).

steps.thinking: In part (a), substitute the known opposite pair $(a, A) = (10, 45^\circ)$ and $B = 60^\circ$ into $\frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{a}{\sin A}$.
In part (b), use $\frac{\sin Q}{q} = \frac{\sin P}{p}$ to evaluate $\sin Q$.
Since $\sin Q = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$, check both $Q_1 = 60^\circ$ and $Q_2 = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$ against $P + Q < 180^\circ$.

now_you_try.problem: In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 30^\circ$, $C = 45^\circ$, and $a = 8\text{ cm}$. Find the exact length of side $c$.

worked_examples.title: Using the Cosine Rule to Find an Unknown Side and an Unknown Angle
worked_examples.problem: (a) In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 5\text{ cm}$, $b = 8\text{ cm}$, and the included angle is $C = 60^\circ$. Find the exact length of side $c$. (b) A triangle has side lengths $a = 3\text{ cm}$, $b = 5\text{ cm}$, and $c = 7\text{ cm}$. Find the size of the largest angle $C$.

steps.thinking: In part (a), substitute $a = 5$, $b = 8$, and $C = 60^\circ$ ($\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$) into $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$.
In part (b), the largest angle is opposite the longest side $c = 7\text{ cm}$. Substitute $a = 3, b = 5, c = 7$ into $\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}$.
Since $\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\cos C = -\frac{1}{2}$ is negative, $C$ is the second-quadrant obtuse supplement $180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$.

now_you_try.problem: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 7\text{ m}$, $b = 8\text{ m}$, and the included angle is $C = 60^\circ$. Find the exact length of side $c$.

worked_examples.title: Triangle Area Formula and Land Surveying
worked_examples.problem: A triangular paddock in Gippsland has two boundary fences of lengths $a = 120\text{ m}$ and $b = 150\text{ m}$ that meet at an included corner angle of $C = 150^\circ$. Find: (a) the area of the paddock in square metres, and (b) the exact length $c$ of the third boundary fence.

steps.thinking: Use the Cosine Rule $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos 150^\circ$, noting that $\cos 150^\circ = -\cos 30^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

now_you_try.problem: Find the exact area of a triangle with two sides of lengths $10\text{ cm}$ and $14\text{ cm}$ and an included angle of $60^\circ$.

common_misconceptions.title: Subtracting $2ab$ from $a^2 + b^2$ Before Multiplying by $\cos C$ (Order of Operations)
common_misconceptions.misconception: In $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$, computing $(a^2 + b^2 - 2ab)$ first and then multiplying the entire result by $\cos C$.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: By order of operations (BIDMAS), $2ab\cos C$ is a single product that must be evaluated before subtracting from $a^2 + b^2$.
common_misconceptions.counter_example: When $C = 90^\circ$ ($\cos 90^\circ = 0$), the incorrect method gives $c^2 = (a^2 + b^2 - 2ab) \times 0 = 0$, whereas the true hypotenuse is $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.

common_misconceptions.title: Forgetting the Obtuse Angle Solution in the Sine Rule Ambiguous Case
common_misconceptions.misconception: Assuming that $\arcsin(k)$ on a calculator always gives the only possible angle in a non-right-angled triangle.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: Because $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$, an inverse sine calculation returns only the acute angle $\theta_1 \in (0^\circ, 90^\circ)$. Whenever the side opposite the unknown angle is longer than the side opposite the given acute angle, $180^\circ - \theta_1$ is a second valid obtuse solution.
common_misconceptions.incorrect_working: $$\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2} \implies \theta = 30^\circ \text{ only} \quad \text{(Incomplete when obtuse triangle is possible)}$$
common_misconceptions.counter_example: A triangle with sides $a = 6$, $b = 6\sqrt{3}$ and angle $A = 30^\circ$ can be drawn with either $B = 60^\circ$ (acute) or $B = 120^\circ$ (obtuse).

fluency_and_understanding.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 30^\circ$, $B = 45^\circ$, and $b = 12\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}$. Find the length of side $a$.
step_by_step_solution: Apply the Sine Rule: $\frac{a}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{12\sqrt{2}}{\sin 45^\circ}$.
Substitute $\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\sin 45^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$: $a = \frac{12\sqrt{2} \times \frac{1}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} = 12\text{ cm}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 6\text{ cm}$, $b = 10\text{ cm}$, and the included angle is $C = 60^\circ$. Find the exact length of side $c$ using the Cosine Rule.
step_by_step_solution: Take the positive square root: $c = \sqrt{76} = 2\sqrt{19}\text{ cm}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Find the area of $\triangle PQR$ given $p = 16\text{ cm}$, $q = 9\text{ cm}$, and included angle $R = 30^\circ$.
step_by_step_solution: Substitute $p = 16$, $q = 9$, and $R = 30^\circ$ into $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}pq\sin R$.
Evaluate $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 9 \times \frac{1}{2} = 36\text{ cm}^2$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: A triangle has side lengths $a = 7\text{ cm}$, $b = 8\text{ cm}$, and $c = 5\text{ cm}$. Use the Cosine Rule to find the exact size of angle $C$ opposite the $5\text{ cm}$ side.
fluency_and_understanding.final_answer: $C = 38.21^\circ$ (where $\cos C = \frac{11}{14}$); and for angle $A$ opposite $a = 7\text{ cm}$, $A = 60^\circ$
step_by_step_solution: Substitute $a = 7, b = 8, c = 5$ into $\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} = \frac{49 + 64 - 25}{2(7)(8)} = \frac{88}{112} = \frac{11}{14} \implies C \approx 38.21^\circ$.
Note also that for angle $A$ opposite $a = 7\text{ cm}$, $\cos A = \frac{8^2 + 5^2 - 7^2}{2(8)(5)} = \frac{40}{80} = \frac{1}{2} \implies A = 60^\circ$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: Two bushfire spotter towers $A$ and $B$ in the Victorian Alps are $10\text{ km}$ apart along an East-West ridge. A smoke plume $S$ is sighted from $A$ and $B$ such that inside $\triangle ABS$, $\angle SAB = 45^\circ$ and $\angle SBA = 75^\circ$. Find (a) $\angle ASB$, and (b) the exact distance $BS$ from tower $B$ to the smoke plume.
step_by_step_solution: By the angle sum of $\triangle ABS$, $\angle ASB = 180^\circ - (45^\circ + 75^\circ) = 60^\circ$.

Apply the Sine Rule: $\frac{BS}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{10}{\sin 60^\circ} \implies BS = \frac{10 \times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = \frac{10\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{10\sqrt{6}}{3}\text{ km}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A yacht leaves Port Phillip Heads ($O$), sails $8\text{ km}$ on a true bearing of $020^\circ\text{T}$ to marker $A$, and then sails $15\text{ km}$ on a true bearing of $140^\circ\text{T}$ to marker $B$. Find (a) the interior angle $\angle OAB$ of $\triangle OAB$, and (b) the straight-line distance $OB$ from Port Phillip Heads to marker $B$.
step_by_step_solution: At marker $A$, the back-bearing to $O$ is $020^\circ + 180^\circ = 200^\circ\text{T}$, while the forward bearing to $B$ is $140^\circ\text{T}$, so the included angle is $\angle OAB = 200^\circ - 140^\circ = 60^\circ$.
Apply the Cosine Rule in $\triangle OAB$: $OB^2 = 8^2 + 15^2 - 2(8)(15)\cos 60^\circ = 64 + 225 - 120 = 169 \implies OB = 13\text{ km}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius $r = 6\text{ cm}$ (so it consists of $6$ congruent equilateral triangles of side $6\text{ cm}$ meeting at the centre with central angles of $60^\circ$). Use the triangle area formula to find the exact total area of the regular hexagon.
step_by_step_solution: Each of the $6$ sectors is a triangle with $a = 6\text{ cm}, b = 6\text{ cm}$, and included angle $C = 60^\circ$, so $A_{\text{triangle}} = \frac{1}{2}(6)(6)\sin 60^\circ = 9\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$.
Multiply by $6$: $A_{\text{hexagon}} = 6 \times 9\sqrt{3} = 54\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: An acute-angled triangle has sides $a = 8\text{ cm}$ and $b = 10\text{ cm}$, and its area is $20\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$. Find (a) the size of the acute included angle $C$, and (b) the exact length of the third side $c$.
step_by_step_solution: Use $\frac{1}{2}(8)(10)\sin C = 20\sqrt{3} \implies 40\sin C = 20\sqrt{3} \implies \sin C = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$; since the triangle is acute-angled, $C = 60^\circ$.
Apply the Cosine Rule: $c^2 = 8^2 + 10^2 - 2(8)(10)\cos 60^\circ = 64 + 100 - 80 = 84 \implies c = \sqrt{84} = 2\sqrt{21}\text{ cm}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 30^\circ$, $b = 10\text{ cm}$, and $a = 5\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}$. Show that the ambiguous case of the Sine Rule produces two distinct triangles, and find the difference between the two possible values of $\angle C$.
step_by_step_solution: By the Sine Rule, $\frac{\sin B}{10} = \frac{\sin 30^\circ}{5\sqrt{2}} \implies \sin B = \frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, which gives $B_1 = 45^\circ$ or $B_2 = 135^\circ$.
Then $C_1 = 180^\circ - (30^\circ + 45^\circ) = 105^\circ$ and $C_2 = 180^\circ - (30^\circ + 135^\circ) = 15^\circ$, so $C_1 - C_2 = 105^\circ - 15^\circ = 90^\circ$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Use the Cosine Rule $\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}$ to explain why a triangle with side lengths $a, b, c$ (where $c$ is the longest side) is: (i) acute-angled if $a^2 + b^2 > c^2$, (ii) right-angled if $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, and (iii) obtuse-angled if $a^2 + b^2 < c^2$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Since $2ab > 0$, the sign of $\cos C$ matches the sign of $a^2 + b^2 - c^2$: positive ($0^\circ < C < 90^\circ$), zero ($C = 90^\circ$), or negative ($90^\circ < C < 180^\circ$)
step_by_step_solution: Because side lengths $a, b > 0$, the denominator $2ab$ in $\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}$ is strictly positive.
Thus $\cos C > 0 \iff a^2 + b^2 > c^2$ ($C$ acute), $\cos C = 0 \iff a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ ($C = 90^\circ$), and $\cos C < 0 \iff a^2 + b^2 < c^2$ ($C$ obtuse).

reasoning_and_communication.question: In a circle of radius $R = 9\text{ cm}$, a chord $AB$ subtends a central angle of $\angle AOB = 120^\circ$ at the centre $O$. Find the exact area of the minor segment cut off by chord $AB$ (i.e. sector area minus $\triangle AOB$ area).
step_by_step_solution: The sector area is $A_{\text{sector}} = \frac{120^\circ}{360^\circ}\pi(9)^2 = 27\pi\text{ cm}^2$.

The triangle area is $A_{\triangle AOB} = \frac{1}{2}(9)(9)\sin 120^\circ = \frac{81}{2} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{81\sqrt{3}}{4}\text{ cm}^2$, so $A_{\text{segment}} = 27\pi - \frac{81\sqrt{3}}{4}\text{ cm}^2$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 13\text{ cm}$, $b = 14\text{ cm}$, and $c = 15\text{ cm}$. Use the Cosine Rule to show that $\cos C = \frac{5}{13}$, then use the identity $\sin^2 C + \cos^2 C = 1$ to show that $\sin C = \frac{12}{13}$, and hence find the exact area of $\triangle ABC$.
step_by_step_solution: Then $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C = \frac{1}{2}(13)(14)\left(\frac{12}{13}\right) = 7 \times 12 = 84\text{ cm}^2$.
